chapters.title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: And so Ivan Ilych went on living for seventeen years after his marriage. By now he was a Public Prosecutor of long experience, and he had turned down a few offered transfers while he held out for a more attractive post. Then something unexpected and unwelcome happened that threw the whole calm rhythm of his life off course. He had been counting on being made presiding judge in a university town, but somehow a man named Happe pushed ahead of him and landed the appointment instead. Ivan Ilych grew bitter, blamed Happe, and got into quarrels with him and with his own superiors as well, who then cooled toward him and skipped over him again when the next round of appointments came up.

This was 1880, the worst year of Ivan Ilych's life. Two things became plain that year. First, his salary was no longer enough for the family to live on. Second, everyone had simply forgotten him, and not only that, the thing he felt as the cruelest, most monstrous injustice struck everyone else as perfectly ordinary. Even his own father saw no reason to lend a hand. Ivan Ilych felt that the whole world had deserted him, and that they all considered a man living on a salary of 3,500 rubles to be in a perfectly normal, even lucky, position. He alone knew the truth: that between the injustices he had suffered, his wife's constant nagging, and the debts he had run up by spending beyond his means, his situation was anything but normal.

To economize that summer he took a leave of absence and went to stay with his wife at her brother's place in the country. There, with no work to occupy him, he felt boredom for the first time in his life, and not just boredom but a depression he could hardly stand. He decided he could not go on like this, that something drastic had to be done. After spending a sleepless night pacing back and forth on the veranda, he resolved to go to Petersburg and stir things up, both to make those who had failed to value him pay for it and to get himself transferred to a different ministry.

The next day, over the loud objections of his wife and her brother, he left for Petersburg with a single goal: to land a post paying five thousand rubles a year. He no longer cared which department it was in, what its leanings were, or what kind of work it involved. All he wanted now was an appointment somewhere that paid five thousand rubles, whether in the civil administration, the banks, the railways, one of the Empress Marya's Institutions, or even the customs service. The two requirements were fixed: a salary of five thousand rubles, and a ministry other than the one that had failed to appreciate him.

And this campaign of Ivan Ilych's met with a striking and unforeseen success. At Kursk an acquaintance of his, F. I. Ilyin, climbed into the first-class carriage, took the seat beside him, and told him about a telegram the governor of Kursk had just received: the ministry was about to be shaken up, and Peter Ivanovich was to be replaced by Ivan Semonovich.

Beyond what it meant for Russia as a whole, this shake-up carried particular weight for Ivan Ilych, because it would push forward a new man, Peter Petrovich, and along with him his friend Zachar Ivanovich. That was very much to Ivan Ilych's advantage, since Zachar Ivanovich was a friend and colleague of his.

In Moscow the news was confirmed, and once he reached Petersburg Ivan Ilych tracked down Zachar Ivanovich and came away with a firm promise of a post in his old Department of Justice. A week later he wired his wife: "Zachar has Miller's place. I get the appointment as soon as I present my report."

Thanks to this reshuffling of personnel, Ivan Ilych had landed, against all expectation, a post in his former ministry that put him two grades above his old colleagues, on top of which it carried a salary of five thousand rubles plus another three thousand five hundred for relocation expenses. All his resentment toward his old enemies and toward the whole department melted away, and Ivan Ilych was perfectly happy.

He went back to the country in higher spirits and better contentment than he had felt in a long while. Praskovya Fedorovna brightened up too, and the two of them called a truce. Ivan Ilych described how everyone in Petersburg had made a fuss over him, how all the men who had been his enemies were now humiliated and fawned on him, how they envied his appointment, and how popular he had been with everyone in the city.

Praskovya Fedorovna listened to all of it and seemed to believe him. She contradicted nothing; she simply went on making plans for their life in the town they were moving to. To Ivan Ilych's delight, her plans turned out to be exactly his plans, that he and his wife were in agreement, and that after this brief stumble his life was getting back its rightful, natural quality of pleasant ease and good form.

Ivan Ilych had only come back for a short while, since he had to begin his new duties on the tenth of September. Besides, he needed time to settle into the new town, to have all his belongings shipped from the province, and to buy and order a great many extra things. In short, he had to set up everything as he had decided to, which lined up almost exactly with what Praskovya Fedorovna had decided on too.

Now that things had fallen out so well, that he and his wife shared the same aims, and that they saw so little of each other, they got along better than they had since the early years of marriage. Ivan Ilych had thought of bringing his whole family along with him right away, but his wife's brother and sister-in-law, who had suddenly turned remarkably warm and friendly toward him and the family, urged him to go on ahead alone.

So he went ahead, and the good mood that came from his success and from the new harmony with his wife, each feeding the other, stayed with him. He found a wonderful house, exactly the kind he and his wife had both dreamed of. Roomy, high-ceilinged reception rooms in the old style, a comfortable and dignified study, separate rooms for his wife and daughter, a study for his son: it was as if the place had been built to order for them. Ivan Ilych oversaw the work himself, picked out the wallpapers, added to the furniture (favoring antiques, which he thought especially in good taste), and supervised the upholstering. Everything kept moving along, drawing nearer and nearer to the picture he had in his mind, and even half-finished it surpassed what he had hoped for. He could already see the refined, elegant character, free of anything vulgar, that the whole place would have once it was done. As he fell asleep he imagined how the reception room would look. Standing in the unfinished drawing room he could already see the fireplace, the screen, the what-not, the little chairs scattered about, the dishes and plates on the walls, and the bronzes, all just where they would go once everything was in place. He took pleasure in imagining how his wife and daughter, who shared his taste in such matters, would be struck by it. They were certainly not expecting anything so fine. He had been especially lucky in finding, and buying cheaply, antiques that gave the whole house a particularly aristocratic air. In his letters, though, he deliberately played everything down so that he could surprise them. It all absorbed him so completely that his new duties, much as he liked his official work, held less of his interest than he had expected. Sometimes during court sessions his mind would wander and he would catch himself wondering whether to have straight or curved cornices for his curtains. He was so taken up with it all that he often did the work himself, shifting the furniture around or rehanging the curtains. Once, when he had climbed a step-ladder to show the upholsterer, who couldn't grasp it, how he wanted the drapes hung, he missed his footing and slipped. Being strong and agile, he caught himself and only banged his side against the knob of the window frame. The bruise was sore, but the pain soon faded, and he felt particularly fit and cheerful just then. He wrote: "I feel fifteen years younger." He had thought he would have everything finished by September, but it dragged on into the middle of October. Still, the result was charming, and not only to his own eyes but to everyone who saw it.

In truth it was exactly what you find in the homes of people of modest means who want to look rich and so end up merely resembling all the other people just like them: there were the damasks, the dark wood, the plants, the rugs, the bronzes both dull and polished, all the things that people of a certain class acquire in order to look like the rest of their class. His house was so like everyone else's that no one would ever have noticed it, yet to him it all seemed quite remarkable. He was overjoyed when he met his family at the station and brought them to the newly furnished house, lit up from end to end, where a footman in a white tie opened the door into the hall full of plants. Then they moved on through the drawing-room and the study, gasping with delight. He led them everywhere, drinking in their praise, glowing with pleasure. Over tea that evening, when Praskovya Fedorovna asked him among other things about his fall, he laughed and acted out how he had gone flying and scared the upholsterer half to death.

"Lucky I'm a bit of an athlete. Another man might have been killed, but I only knocked myself, right here; it hurts when you touch it, but it's already wearing off, it's just a bruise." So they settled into their new home, where, as always happens, once they were fully moved in they discovered they were just one room short, and with the larger income, which, as always, fell just a little short, by some five hundred rubles, but on the whole everything was very pleasant.

Things went especially well at first, while everything was not yet finally in place and there was still something left to do: this thing to buy, that one to order, another to be moved, something else to be adjusted. There were some squabbles between husband and wife, but both of them were so pleased and had so much to keep them busy that it all blew over without any serious quarrels. Once there was nothing left to arrange, life became a little flat, and something seemed to be missing, but by then they were making acquaintances, settling into routines, and life was filling out.

Ivan Ilych spent his mornings at the law court and came home to dinner, and at first he was generally in good spirits, though now and then the house itself would put him out of temper. (Every stain on the tablecloth or the upholstery, every snapped window-blind cord set him off. He had poured so much effort into arranging it all that any damage to it pained him.) But on the whole his life ran the way he believed a life should run: easily, pleasantly, with proper decorum. He rose at nine, drank his coffee, read the paper, then put on his undress uniform and went off to the law courts. There the harness he worked in had already been broken in to fit him, and he slipped into it without the slightest snag: petitioners, inquiries at the chancery, the chancery itself, the public and administrative sittings. Through all of this the trick was to shut out anything fresh and alive, which always disrupts the smooth running of official business, and to permit only official dealings with people, and even those only on official grounds. Suppose a man came in wanting some information. If the matter fell outside Ivan Ilych's sphere, he would have nothing to do with him. But if the man had business with him in his official capacity, something that could be set down on officially stamped paper, then he would do everything, absolutely everything he could within the bounds of such dealings, and while doing it he would keep up the appearance of friendly human relations, that is, he would observe the ordinary courtesies. The moment the official relationship ended, so did everything else. Ivan Ilych had this gift of separating his real life from the official side of things, of keeping the two from mixing, to the highest degree, and through long practice and natural talent he had perfected it to the point where sometimes, like a virtuoso, he would even let himself allow the human and the official to blend a little. He let himself do this precisely because he knew he could, at any moment he chose, snap back into the strictly official manner and drop the human one. And he did it all easily, pleasantly, correctly, even with a certain artistry. Between sittings he smoked, drank tea, chatted a bit about politics, a bit about general matters, a bit about cards, but most of all about official appointments. Tired, but with the satisfaction of a virtuoso, one of the first violins who has played his part in the orchestra flawlessly, he would come home to find that his wife and daughter had been out paying calls or had a visitor, and that his son had been to school, done his homework with his tutor, and was no doubt learning whatever it is they teach at the High Schools. Everything was as it should be. After dinner, if there were no guests, Ivan Ilych would sometimes read a book that was being much talked about at the moment, and in the evening he settled down to work, that is, he went over official papers, compared the testimony of witnesses, and matched up the relevant paragraphs of the Code. This was neither dull nor entertaining. It was dull when he might otherwise have been playing bridge, but if there was no bridge to be had, it was at least better than doing nothing or sitting with his wife. Ivan Ilych's great pleasure was giving small dinners to which he invited men and women of good social standing, and just as his drawing-room looked like every other drawing-room, so his pleasant little parties looked like every other such party.

Once they even gave a dance. Ivan Ilych enjoyed it, and the whole thing came off well, except that it touched off a furious quarrel with his wife over the cakes and sweets. Praskovya Fedorovna had her own plans, but Ivan Ilych insisted on getting everything from an expensive confectioner and ordered far too many cakes, and the quarrel broke out because some of the cakes were left over and the confectioner's bill came to forty-five rubles. It was a big, ugly fight. Praskovya Fedorovna called him "a fool and an idiot," and he clutched his head and made furious hints about divorce.

But the dance itself had been a pleasure. The best people were there, and Ivan Ilych had danced with Princess Trufonova, sister of the woman who had founded the well-known society called "Bear My Burden." The pleasures tied to his work were pleasures of ambition; his social pleasures were pleasures of vanity; but Ivan Ilych's keenest pleasure of all was playing bridge. He admitted that no matter what disagreeable thing came up in his life, the one pleasure that shone out above everything else, like a beam of light, was to sit down to bridge with good players, partners who weren't loud, and of course at a four-handed table (with five players it was a nuisance to have to sit out, even if you pretended not to mind), to play a sharp, serious game (when the cards allowed), and then to have supper and a glass of wine. After a game of bridge, especially when he had won a little (winning a large amount was unpleasant), Ivan Ilych went to bed in particularly good spirits.

And so they lived. They built up a circle of acquaintances among the best people and were visited by important figures and by younger folk. In their judgments about whom to know, husband, wife, and daughter were in complete agreement, and without ever discussing it they were of one mind in keeping at a distance and brushing off the various shabby friends and relations who, with a great display of affection, would come gushing into the drawing-room with its Japanese plates on the walls. Before long these shabby friends stopped pushing themselves forward, and only the best people were left in the Golovins' set.

Young men began paying court to Lisa, and one of them, Petrishchev, an examining magistrate and the son and sole heir of Dmitri Ivanovich Petrishchev, grew so attentive to her that Ivan Ilych had already raised the matter with Praskovya Fedorovna and was wondering whether they ought to arrange a party for the young people, or perhaps put on some amateur theatricals.
So they lived, and everything went smoothly, without change, and life flowed along pleasantly.

chapters.title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: They were all in good health. You couldn't really call it ill health when Ivan Ilych occasionally mentioned that he had an odd taste in his mouth and felt some discomfort on his left side. But this discomfort grew, and though it never quite became pain, it turned into a constant sense of pressure in his side, paired with a sour mood. His irritability got steadily worse and began to spoil the agreeable, easy, proper life the Golovin family had built. Quarrels between husband and wife grew more and more frequent, until before long the ease and pleasantness were gone and even the appearance of decorum was barely kept up. Scenes became common again, and very few of those calm little islets were left where husband and wife could meet without an outburst. Now Praskovya Fedorovna had real grounds for saying that her husband had a difficult temper. With her usual gift for exaggeration, she claimed he had always had a dreadful temper, and that it had taken all her good nature to bear with it for twenty years. It was true that now the quarrels were started by him. His flare-ups always came right before dinner, often just as he started on his soup. Sometimes he would notice that a plate or dish was chipped, or that the food wasn't right, or that his son had his elbow on the table, or that his daughter's hair wasn't done the way he liked, and for every bit of it he blamed Praskovya Fedorovna. At first she fought back and said cutting things to him, but two or three times he flew into such a rage at the start of dinner that she realized it was caused by some physical disorder set off by eating. So she held herself in and stopped answering, and just hurried to get the meal over with. She considered this self-control highly commendable. Having concluded that her husband had a dreadful temper and was making her life miserable, she began to feel sorry for herself, and the more she pitied herself the more she hated him. She started wishing he would die, yet she didn't actually want him dead, because then his salary would stop. And this only made her angrier with him. She thought herself terribly unfortunate precisely because not even his death could rescue her, and although she hid her bitterness, that buried bitterness of hers fed his irritation in turn. After one scene in which Ivan Ilych had been particularly unjust, and after which he had explained that he certainly was irritable but that it was because he wasn't well, she told him that if he was ill he ought to do something about it, and insisted he go see a famous doctor. He went. Everything unfolded just as he had expected, just as it always does. There was the usual wait and the air of importance the doctor put on, which Ivan Ilych knew so well (it was the very air he himself put on in court), and the tapping and listening, and the questions whose answers were a foregone conclusion and obviously unnecessary, and the look of consequence that said, "Just put yourself in our hands and we'll arrange everything; we know beyond any doubt how it must be done, always the same way for everyone alike." It was exactly like the law courts. The doctor put on toward him precisely the same air that he himself put on toward an accused man.

The doctor explained that such-and-such a sign pointed to such-and-such inside the patient, but that if the examination of such-and-such failed to confirm it, then he would have to assume this and that. And if he assumed this and that, then... and so on. For Ivan Ilych only one question mattered: was his case serious or not? But the doctor brushed that unwelcome question aside. From his point of view it wasn't the question at issue; the real question was to decide among a floating kidney, chronic catarrh, or an inflamed appendix. It wasn't a matter of Ivan Ilych's life or death, but of choosing between a floating kidney and the appendix. And that question the doctor settled brilliantly, as it seemed to Ivan Ilych, in favor of the appendix, with the proviso that if a urine analysis turned up fresh evidence, the matter would be looked at again. All of this was exactly what Ivan Ilych himself had done brilliantly a thousand times with the men on trial before him. The doctor delivered his summing-up just as brilliantly, peering over his spectacles at the accused with an air of triumph, even cheerfulness. From the doctor's summing-up Ivan Ilych gathered that things were bad, but that to the doctor, and probably to everyone else, it was a matter of indifference, whereas for him it was bad. And this realization struck him hard, filling him with a vast pity for himself and a bitterness at the doctor's indifference to a matter of such importance.

He said nothing of all this. He simply rose, laid the doctor's fee on the table, and remarked with a sigh, "We sick people probably ask the wrong questions a good deal. But tell me, in general terms, is this complaint dangerous or not?"

The doctor gave him a stern look over his spectacles with one eye, as if to say, "Prisoner, if you won't confine yourself to the questions put to you, I'll be obliged to have you removed from the court." "I have already told you what I think necessary and proper. The analysis may show something further." And the doctor bowed.

Ivan Ilych went out slowly, climbed dejectedly into his sledge, and drove home. The whole way home he turned over what the doctor had said, trying to translate all those tangled, murky, scientific phrases into plain words and to read in them some answer to the question, "Is my condition bad? Is it very bad? Or is there as yet nothing much the matter?" And it seemed to him that the gist of what the doctor had said was that it was very bad indeed. Everything in the streets looked dismal to him. The cabmen, the houses, the people passing by, the shops, all of it was gloomy. This ache, this dull, gnawing ache that never let up for an instant, seemed to have taken on a new and graver meaning from the doctor's evasive remarks. Ivan Ilych now watched it with a new and oppressive dread.

He got home and started telling his wife about it. She listened, but partway through his account his daughter came in with her hat on, ready to go out with her mother. She sat down reluctantly to hear this dreary story, but she couldn't stand it for long, and the mother didn't hear him out to the end either.

"Well, I'm very glad," she said. "Now be sure you take your medicine regularly. Give me the prescription and I'll send Gerasim to the chemist's." And off she went to get ready to go out. The whole time she was in the room Ivan Ilych had barely dared to breathe, and he let out a deep sigh once she had gone.
"Well," he thought, "maybe it isn't so bad after all."

He began taking his medicine and following the doctor's instructions, which had been changed after the urine was examined. But then it turned out that there was a contradiction between what the urine analysis indicated and the symptoms that were actually showing up. What was happening to him didn't match what the doctor had told him, and either the doctor had forgotten something, or blundered, or kept something back from him. Still, he couldn't really be blamed, and Ivan Ilych went on obeying his orders to the letter, and at first he took some comfort in doing so.

From the time of that visit to the doctor, Ivan Ilych's main occupation became the precise carrying-out of the doctor's instructions about hygiene and medicine, and the close watching of his pain and his bodily functions. His chief interest now turned to people's ailments and people's health. Whenever illnesses, deaths, or recoveries were mentioned in his hearing, especially when the illness resembled his own, he would listen with an agitation he tried to hide, ask questions, and apply what he heard to his own case.

The pain did not ease, but Ivan Ilych kept forcing himself to believe he was getting better. And he managed to believe it as long as nothing upset him. But the moment he had any friction with his wife, any setback at work, or a bad hand at bridge, he was instantly and sharply aware of his disease. In the past he had endured such mishaps, confident he would soon set right whatever was wrong, overcome it, win through, make a grand slam. Now every little misfortune knocked him flat and threw him into despair. He would say to himself, "There now, just as I was starting to get better and the medicine had begun to work, along comes this cursed misfortune, this aggravation..." And he would rage at the mishap, or at the people who were causing the aggravation and killing him, for he could feel that this rage was killing him, yet he couldn't hold it back. You'd think it would have been obvious to him that this fury with circumstances and people was making his illness worse, and that he ought therefore to pay no attention to unpleasant happenings. But he drew the exact opposite conclusion: he told himself that what he needed was peace and quiet, and so he watched out for anything that might disturb it and grew irritable at the slightest threat to it. His condition was made worse by the fact that he read medical books and consulted doctors. The disease advanced so gradually that he could deceive himself when he compared one day with the next; the difference was so tiny. But whenever he consulted the doctors, it seemed to him that he was getting worse, and even very fast. And yet, in spite of this, he kept on consulting them.

That month he went to see another celebrated doctor, who told him almost the same thing as the first, only put his questions a little differently, and the visit to this celebrity only deepened Ivan Ilych's doubts and fears. A doctor who was a friend of a friend, a very good one, diagnosed his illness yet again, quite differently from the rest, and although he predicted a recovery, his questions and conjectures left Ivan Ilych more bewildered than ever and made his doubts worse. A homeopath diagnosed it in still another way and prescribed a medicine that Ivan Ilych took in secret for a week. But after a week, feeling no improvement and having lost faith in both this treatment and the earlier doctor's, he sank into deeper gloom. One day a lady he knew told him about a cure brought about by a miracle-working icon. Ivan Ilych caught himself listening intently and starting to believe it had really happened. This frightened him. "Has my mind really gone so soft?" he asked himself. "Nonsense! It's all rubbish. I mustn't give in to nervous fears; having picked a doctor I must stick strictly to his treatment. That's what I'll do. There, it's settled. I won't dwell on it; I'll follow the treatment seriously until summer, and then we'll see. No more of this wavering from now on!" That was easy to say and impossible to do. The pain in his side wore him down and seemed to grow worse and more relentless, while the taste in his mouth grew stranger and stranger. It seemed to him that his breath had a foul smell, and he noticed that he was losing his appetite and his strength. There was no fooling himself: something terrible, something new, something more important than anything else in his whole life was happening inside him, and he alone knew about it. The people around him either didn't understand or wouldn't, and thought everything in the world was carrying on as usual. That tormented Ivan Ilych more than anything. He could see that his household, above all his wife and daughter, who were in a perfect frenzy of social calls, understood none of it and were annoyed that he was so glum and so demanding, as though it were his fault. Try as they might to hide it, he saw that he was an obstacle in their way, and that his wife had settled on a fixed attitude toward his illness and held to it no matter what he said or did. Her line was this: "You know," she would tell her friends, "Ivan Ilych simply can't do what other people do and follow the treatment he's been given. One day he'll take his drops and stick to his diet and go to bed on time, and the next, unless I keep an eye on him, he'll forget his medicine, eat sturgeon, which is forbidden, and stay up playing cards until one in the morning."
"Oh, come now, when did I do that?" Ivan Ilych would ask in annoyance. "Only once, at Peter Ivanovich's."
"And yesterday with Shebek."
"Well, even if I hadn't stayed up, this pain would have kept me awake anyway."
"Be that as it may, you'll never get well that way; you'll just go on making the rest of us miserable."

Praskovya Fedorovna's attitude toward Ivan Ilych's illness, as she put it both to others and to him, was that it was his own fault and just one more of the annoyances he heaped on her. Ivan Ilych could tell that this came out of her without her meaning it, but that didn't make it any easier to bear.

At the law courts, too, Ivan Ilych noticed, or thought he noticed, a strange attitude toward him. Sometimes it seemed to him that people were eyeing him with curiosity, as a man whose position might soon be open. At other times his friends would suddenly start ribbing him in a friendly way about his low spirits, as though the dreadful, horrifying, unheard-of thing that was going on inside him, endlessly gnawing at him and dragging him irresistibly away, were a perfectly amusing topic for jokes. Schwartz especially got on his nerves with his jokiness, his liveliness, his savoir-faire, all of which reminded Ivan Ilych of what he himself had been ten years before.

Friends came over to make up a table, and they sat down to cards. They dealt, bending the new cards to soften them, and he sorted out the diamonds in his hand and found he had seven. His partner bid "No trumps" and backed him with two diamonds. What more could you ask for? It ought to have been cheerful and lively. They were going to make a grand slam. But all at once Ivan Ilych became aware of that gnawing pain, that taste in his mouth, and it struck him as absurd that under such circumstances he could feel glad about making a grand slam.

He glanced at his partner, Mikhail Mikhaylovich, who rapped the table with his strong hand and, instead of grabbing up the tricks, politely and considerately pushed the cards toward Ivan Ilych so that he could have the pleasure of gathering them in without the bother of reaching for them. "Does he think I'm too weak to stretch out my arm?" thought Ivan Ilych, and, losing track of what he was doing, he over-trumped his partner and threw away the grand slam by three tricks. And the most appalling part of it was that he could see how upset Mikhail Mikhaylovich was, and yet he himself didn't care. And it was dreadful to realize why he didn't care.

They all saw that he was suffering and said, "We can stop if you're tired. Take a rest." Lie down? No, he wasn't in the least tired, and he finished out the rubber. Everyone was gloomy and silent. Ivan Ilych felt that he had spread this gloom over them and that he couldn't shake it off. They had supper and went home, and Ivan Ilych was left alone with the awareness that his life had been poisoned and was poisoning the lives of others, and that this poison wasn't fading but was sinking deeper and deeper into his whole being.

And with this awareness, and the physical pain on top of the terror, he had to go to bed, often to lie awake most of the night. The next morning he had to get up again, dress, go to the law courts, speak, write; or, if he stayed in, spend at home all twenty-four hours of a day, each of which was a torment. And he had to live like this, utterly alone, on the edge of a chasm, with no one who understood or pitied him.

chapters.title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: So one month went by, and then another. Just before the New Year his brother-in-law came to town and stayed at their house. Ivan Ilych was at the law courts, and Praskovya Fedorovna had gone out shopping. When Ivan Ilych got home and walked into his study, he found his brother-in-law there, a healthy, ruddy-faced man, unpacking his portmanteau himself. He lifted his head at the sound of Ivan Ilych's footsteps and stared at him for a moment without a word. That stare told Ivan Ilych everything. His brother-in-law opened his mouth to let out a cry of surprise, but caught himself, and that very check confirmed it all.
"I've changed, haven't I?"
"Yes, there's a change."

And after that, no matter how hard Ivan Ilych tried to steer his brother-in-law back to the subject of his appearance, the man would say nothing more about it. Praskovya Fedorovna came home, and her brother went out to meet her. Ivan Ilych locked the door and began studying himself in the mirror, first head-on, then in profile. He picked up a photograph of himself with his wife and compared it with what the mirror showed him. The change in him was enormous. Then he bared his arms to the elbow, looked at them, pulled the sleeves back down, sat down on an ottoman, and grew blacker than the night.

"No, no, this won't do!" he said to himself, and he jumped up, went to the table, took up some legal papers, and tried to read them, but he couldn't go on. He unlocked the door and went into the reception room. The door to the drawing-room was shut. He crept up to it on tiptoe and listened.
"No, you're exaggerating!" Praskovya Fedorovna was saying.
"Exaggerating! Can't you see it? Why, the man's as good as dead. Look at his eyes, there's no life in them. But what is it that's actually wrong with him?"
"Nobody knows. Nikolaevich said something, but I couldn't make out what. And Leshchetitsky said just the opposite..."

Ivan Ilych moved away, went to his own room, lay down, and fell to brooding: "The kidney, a floating kidney." He remembered everything the doctors had told him about how it came loose and drifted around. And by an effort of imagination he tried to grab hold of that kidney and pin it down and prop it up. It would take so little to do it, it seemed to him. "No, I'll go see Peter Ivanovich again." He rang the bell, ordered the carriage, and got himself ready to go.
"Where are you off to, Jean?" his wife asked, with an unusually sad and unusually gentle look. That unusual gentleness irritated him. He looked at her sullenly.
"I have to go see Peter Ivanovich."
He went to see Peter Ivanovich, and the two of them went together to see Peter Ivanovich's friend the doctor. The doctor was in, and Ivan Ilych had a long talk with him.
Going over the anatomical and physiological details of what, in the doctor's view, was happening inside him, he understood it all.

There was something, a small thing, in the vermiform appendix. It could all come right. You only had to stimulate one organ into greater activity and quiet down another, and then the absorption would take place and everything would set itself right. He got home rather late for dinner, ate his meal, and chatted cheerfully, but for a long time he couldn't bring himself to go back to work in his room. At last he went to his study and did what had to be done, but the awareness that he had set something aside, an important, private matter that he would come back to once his work was finished, never left him. When he had finished his work, he remembered that this private matter was the thought of his vermiform appendix. But he didn't give in to it; he went to the drawing-room for tea. There were callers, among them the examining magistrate who would make a good match for his daughter, and they were talking, playing the piano, and singing. Ivan Ilych, as Praskovya Fedorovna noticed, spent that evening in better spirits than usual, but he never once forgot that he had postponed the important matter of the appendix. At eleven o'clock he said goodnight and went off to his bedroom. Since his illness he had been sleeping alone in a small room next to his study. He undressed and picked up a novel by Zola, but instead of reading it he sank into thought, and in his mind the wished-for improvement in the vermiform appendix took place. The absorption, the evacuation, the return to normal function. "Yes, that's it!" he said to himself. "You only have to give nature a hand, that's all." He remembered his medicine, got up, took it, and lay down on his back, waiting for the medicine to do its kindly work and ease the pain. "I just have to take it regularly and steer clear of anything harmful. I already feel better, much better." He started touching his side; it didn't hurt to the touch. "There, I really can't feel it. It's much better already." He blew out the light and turned onto his side... "The appendix is getting better, the absorption is happening." Suddenly he felt the old, familiar, dull, gnawing pain, stubborn and grave. There was the same familiar, sickening taste in his mouth. His heart sank and he felt dazed. "My God! My God!" he muttered. "Again, again! And it will never stop." And all at once the whole thing took on a completely different aspect. "Vermiform appendix! Kidney!" he said to himself. "It's not a question of appendix or kidney; it's a question of life and... death. Yes, life was here, and now it's slipping away, slipping away, and I can't hold it back. Yes. Why fool myself? Isn't it plain to everyone but me that I'm dying, and that it's only a matter of weeks, of days? It could happen any moment now. There was light, and now there is darkness. I was here, and now I'm going there. Where?" A chill ran over him, his breathing stopped, and he could feel only the pounding of his heart. "When I no longer exist, what will there be? There will be nothing. Then where will I be once I'm gone? Can this be dying? No, I don't want it!" He sprang up and tried to light the candle, fumbled for it with trembling hands, knocked candle and candlestick onto the floor, and fell back on his pillow.

"What's the point? It makes no difference," he said to himself, staring wide-eyed into the dark. "Death. Yes, death. And not one of them knows or wants to know it, and none of them has any pity for me. They're playing." (Through the door he could hear the faint sound of a song and its accompaniment.) "It's all the same to them, but they'll die too! Fools! Me first, them later, but it'll be the same for them. And here they are, having a merry time... the brutes!"
Rage choked him, and he was wretched, in agony, beyond enduring. "It can't be that all men are condemned to suffer this hideous horror!" He raised himself up.

"Something must be wrong. I have to calm down, I have to think it all through from the start." And he began thinking again. "Yes, the start of my illness: I banged my side, but I was still perfectly well that day and the next. It ached a little, then a bit more. I saw the doctors, then came the gloom and the anguish, more doctors, and I drew closer to the abyss. My strength kept failing, I came nearer and nearer, and now I've wasted away to nothing and there's no light left in my eyes. I keep thinking about the appendix, but this is death! I keep thinking about fixing the appendix, and all the while here is death! Can it really be death?" Terror seized him again and he gasped for air. He leaned down and felt around for the matches, pressing his elbow against the night-stand beside the bed. It was in his way and it hurt him; he got furious with it, pressed down harder still, and knocked it over. Breathless and in despair, he dropped onto his back, expecting death to come any second.
Meanwhile the visitors were leaving. Praskovya Fedorovna was showing them out. She heard something fall and came in.
"What happened?"
"Nothing. I knocked it over by accident."
She went out and came back with a candle. He lay there breathing hard, like a man who has just run a thousand yards, and stared up at her with a fixed gaze.
"What is it, Jean?"

"No... no... thing. I knocked it over." ("What's the use of telling her? She won't understand," he thought.) And in fact she did not understand. She picked up the stand, lit his candle, and hurried off to see another guest out. When she came back he was still lying on his back, looking upward.
"What is it? Do you feel worse?"
"Yes."

She shook her head and sat down. "You know, Jean, I think we'll have to ask Leshchetitsky to come and see you here at home." This meant calling in the famous specialist, no matter the cost. He smiled venomously and said, "No." She stayed a little longer, then came over to him and kissed his forehead. While she was kissing him he hated her with all his soul, and it was all he could do not to shove her away.
"Good night. Please God you'll sleep."
"Yes."
